summary: Creative workers across music, writing, illustration, voice acting and other fields are starting to coordinate their responses to generative AI. Fight for the Future and United Musicians and Allied Workers launched #AIdayofaction, urging Congress to bar corporations from copyrighting AI-made art. The FTC also hosted a cross-industry roundtable where officials and creators discussed the risks of AI to artists' livelihoods and control over their work.
one_line: Artists across creative industries are uniting, through the #AIdayofaction campaign and an FTC roundtable, to push back against corporate misuse of generative AI.
key_facts: Fight for the Future partnered with United Musicians and Allied Workers to launch #AIdayofaction, a campaign calling on Congress to block corporations from obtaining copyrights on music and other art made with AI.
The campaign's logic is that if major record labels cannot copyright AI-assisted music, they will be forced to keep humans in the creative process.

Lia Holland, Fight for the Future's Campaigns and Communications director, says creative fields are 'a little bit siloed' and that the day of action aimed to show shared concerns and create an organizing point.
The campaign hopes AI tools will 'become ways for individual humans to make more money, work less, and compete with the corporations that exploit them.'
Holland says musicians are perhaps more familiar with AI-like tools such as music production software and MIDI drum loops, giving them a more progressive view of technology.
Spotify removed thousands of AI-crafted songs from its platform but also globally launched an AI-powered DJ that curates music and speaks in a synthetic voice.

Universal Music Group said AI training on its artists' music raises the question of whether stakeholders side with artists and human expression or with 'deep fakes, fraud and denying artists their due compensation,' after an AI song imitating Drake and The Weeknd went viral.
The FTC hosted a roundtable this week with voice acting, science fiction, screenwriting, music, illustration and fashion figures on how generative AI affects creatives.
FTC chair Lina Khan warned the technologies could 'virtually overnight' disempower creators who watch their life's work be appropriated into models they cannot control.

Roundtable participants raised concerns about opt-out requirements that by default train AI models on artists' original work, and said existing copyright law could be a useful but not comprehensive tool for guardrails.
A WGA representative said striking writers won their own protections in a new agreement, but the fight 'doesn't stop at the bargaining table.'
FTC commissioner Rebecca Slaughter said 'Art is fundamentally human' and that generative AI 'cannot and will not replace human creativity.'
